title: TF-IDF from scratch
summary: Two separate questions, how much a term matters here and whether it tells you anything at all, multiplied together. IDF is really surprisal, which is why it zeroes out stopwords without a stopword list.
html:
Day 3 left you with a vector of raw counts and a complaint: the biggest numbers sit on the, of, is, so every chunk looks like every other chunk. Today you fix that, and you do it by asking two separate questions instead of one.

  1. Given that this term appears in this chunk, how much does it matter here?
  2. Does this term tell you anything at all, across the whole corpus?

The first is term frequency. The second is inverse document frequency. Multiply them and you have TF-IDF, which has been the baseline text scorer since the early 1970s and is still what you should build first for any new corpus.

Term frequency, and why the raw count is wrong

Start with the obvious version: tf(t, d) is the number of times term t appears in document d. A chunk mentioning queen five times is more about queens than one mentioning it once. Fine so far.

But is a chunk with 20 mentions twenty times more about queens than one with a single mention? Clearly not. Relevance saturates. The first mention tells you the topic. The tenth tells you almost nothing new.

The standard fix is log damping:

tf(t, d) = 1 + log(count(t, d))     when count > 0
         = 0                         when count = 0

Now 1 mention scores 1.0, 2 mentions score 1.69, 10 mentions score 3.30, 100 mentions score 5.61. Growth without runaway. The 1 + exists so that a single occurrence scores 1.0 rather than 0, since log(1) = 0 would otherwise erase every term that appears exactly once, which is most of them.

If you have ever put a log scale on a latency dashboard for the same reason, this is that move.

Inverse document frequency, which is really surprisal

Document frequency df(t) is the number of documents containing term t at least once. Note that it counts documents, not occurrences. A term appearing 500 times inside one document still has df of 1.

Intuitively, a term in every document is useless for telling documents apart, and a rare term is highly informative. Turn that into a number:

idf(t) = log( N / df(t) )        N = total number of documents

There is a nicer way to read this than "inverse frequency". The fraction df(t) / N is the probability that a randomly chosen document contains the term. So idf is -log(P(t)), which in information theory is the surprisal of the term: how many bits you learn when you see it. A term you expect to see teaches you nothing. A term you did not expect teaches you a lot.

That is not a metaphor laid on top afterwards. Karen Sparck Jones proposed IDF in 1972 on essentially that reasoning, and it is why the formula has survived fifty years of people trying to replace it.

Put them together and run the numbers

weight(t, d) = tf(t, d) * idf(t)
             = (1 + log(count(t, d))) * log(N / df(t))

Take a four document corpus so the arithmetic is checkable by hand:

d1: the queen lays the eggs
d2: the worker bees collect nectar
d3: the queen is the only fertile female
d4: nectar becomes honey in the hive

N is 4. Three terms, three very different outcomes:

termdfidf = log(4/df)count in d1tfweight in d1
the4log(1) = 0.00021.6930.000
queen2log(2) = 0.69311.0000.693
eggs1log(4) = 1.38611.0001.386

Look at what happened to the. It is the most frequent word in d1, appearing twice, and its final weight is exactly zero. It appears in every document, so it carries no information, so IDF annihilates it. You did not need a stopword list. The mathematics removed it on its own.

Meanwhile eggs, appearing once, outweighs queen, also appearing once, because eggs is rarer in this corpus. That is the whole idea working.

Where the honesty belongs

TF-IDF is not one formula. It is a family, and the variants genuinely differ:

  • A term appearing in every document gets idf exactly 0 and vanishes completely. Some implementations use log(N / df) + 1 or log(1 + N / df) so ubiquitous terms are merely cheap rather than erased. Scikit-learn does this by default, and its output will not match a textbook formula.
  • Some use log((N - df) / df), the probabilistic form.
  • TF has at least five common variants: raw, log damped, augmented, boolean, length normalised.

The SMART notation from Cornell exists to name these combinations precisely, because by the 1980s nobody could tell whose TF-IDF was whose. If you are comparing your numbers to a paper or a library, check which variant before concluding you have a bug. In practice the choice moves retrieval metrics by a point or two, not by twenty, so pick one and be consistent. Do not spend a week on it.

What TF-IDF still cannot do

Two limits, both of which the course comes back to.

It has no idea that volume and LUN mean the same thing. IDF is computed per surface form. Your vocabulary mismatch from Day 3 is completely untouched. That waits for Day 9.

It ignores document length. A 2000 word chunk has more chances to accumulate weight than a 50 word chunk, purely by being long, so long documents drift to the top for no good reason. Tomorrow's cosine normalisation partly handles this, and BM25 on Day 31 handles it properly with an explicit length term.

You now have weighted vectors. What you do not have is a way to compare two of them, because raw dot products still reward length. That is Day 5, cosine similarity and why we normalize.
exercise:
1. Build it. Write TF-IDF in plain Python, no libraries. Take a list of documents, tokenize by lowercasing and splitting on non-letters, build df with a Counter over sets of terms per document (a common bug is counting occurrences instead of documents), then emit each document as a dict of term to weight. Roughly 25 lines.

2. Check it against the table above. Run it on the four bee documents in this lesson. Confirm the comes out at exactly 0.0 and that eggs outranks queen in d1. If it does not, your df is probably counting occurrences.

3. Point it at something real. Run it over 20 or so files from a repo or doc folder you actually work on, and print the top 5 terms by weight for each file. Read them. Do they describe the file? Where they don't, ask why: is the term too rare to be meaningful, or is the file about something the words don't say? That second case is the vocabulary problem again, and you'll want the example on Day 9.
